title: A day in 2050
description: One ordinary day in 2050 through three families, and the laws behind it: what each one does, when it starts, what it costs and where it falls short.
intro: Picture an ordinary day in 2050, seen through three households. Jordan is a single man in his mid-twenties, learning a trade. Maya and Sam are raising two young children, with Sam's parents a few blocks away. Carol and Dev are getting ready to retire, and their grown son Eli lives with them. Choose whose day you read: each family meets the same laws in its own way.

Every scene below is imagined: the people are composites, not real people, and nothing here is a forecast. But each scene shows something that would be different because of a law Project 2050 would pass, starting in January 2029,{c:plan-start} and each says when that law begins, what it costs, and where it still falls short. Open any scene to see the details, the hard questions and the evidence behind every figure. Each family's day ends with the money: what it all costs and who pays.
reading_key: The people are composites and the town is not a real place. Nothing here is a forecast.
Our analysis, not an official score.
Costs and effects are the project's own estimates on its own models, marked "on our estimates" or "about". No official scorekeeper has scored the plan.
Each scene shows only what its law has started by 2050, and says when each part begins.
A small number after a sentence leads to the passage in the project's records that the figure comes from.
Most of these laws need a supermajority in the Senate or a change to its rules; each scene shows what happens if its law passes.
A few money figures wait on choices the project has not yet made. The page says so where they would go.

principles.title: Freedom you can use
principles.body: A right matters more when you have the time, security and support to exercise it: to care for someone, change jobs, learn, make a home and take part in your community.

principles.title: A society that cares for its people
principles.body: Children should grow up without poverty. Illness, disability and aging should bring dependable support, and the people who give care deserve the pay and respect that make good care possible.

principles.title: Power that answers to people
principles.body: Voting should be easy and secure, money should not drown out citizens, and the officials who serve the public should not profit from what they know.

principles.title: Responsibility across generations
principles.body: Pay honestly for what we promise, say who pays, and leave the next generation a cleaner country and a government that works.

what_changed: A monthly child benefit for working and middle-class families: $300 a month for each child from 6 to 17 and $360 for each child under 6, in 2025 dollars and rising with prices.{c:afa-amounts} Every family below about $150,000 for couples ($112,500 for single parents), adjusted for inflation, gets the full amount, however little the parents earn.{c:afa-phaseout}
It starts from records the government already holds, so families do not have to apply. A parent confirms a letter instead of filling out a form.

Twelve weeks of paid leave for a new child, a family member's serious illness or your own, run by Social Security, paying 85% of the first part of your wages, with your job back if you have been on it at least 90 days, once the 2030 Social Security act passes.{c:leave}{c:leave-start}{c:leave-job}
Workers without children get a real earned income credit from 2030: the 2021 maximum of $1,502, rising with prices since.{c:eitc} Food help cut by the 2025 law is restored.{c:floor-other}

Paid on-ramps into the plan's jobs, in care, construction and repair, rail and transit, housing production and clean power, with a training stipend of up to $9,000 a year in 2030 dollars, rising with prices. It is an offer, never a condition: no benefit depends on taking part.{c:onramps}

A Social Security act in 2030 promises full benefits on time: if a trust fund would run short before the act's new revenue is enough, the general fund lends it the shortfall, repaid with interest. The revenue starts with the 12.4% Social Security tax on earnings above $250,000, from January 2031, and the act adds a stronger minimum benefit and credit for caregiving years.{c:ss-act}
begins: The child benefit, the workers' credit and the paid on-ramps from 2030.{c:floor-start}{c:onramps}
Paid leave from 2031; the contributions that pay for it start in 2030.{c:leave-start}
The Social Security act in 2030; its tax on earnings above $250,000 from January 2031.{c:ss-act}
cost: On our estimates the child benefit costs about $1.85 trillion over 2030-39, and the whole floor about $298 billion in 2040 on the general fund, before the plan's financing.{c:floor-cost}
On our estimates a worker earning $60,000 pays $180 a year toward paid leave to start.{c:leave-cost}
limits: On our estimates child poverty falls to about 9% (somewhere between 8% and 12%), from about 13.5-14.5% under the law as it will stand in 2029. That is a large cut, not an end to child poverty.{c:child-poverty}
Couples above about $210,000 get somewhat less than the credit they would otherwise get.{c:afa-top}
The workers' credit is for low pay: it phases out as earnings rise, so a worker on a steady trade wage gets little or none of it.

questions.q: Won't people stop working?
a: Studies of the monthly payments families got in 2021 found no effect on employment. Even the economists who expect some parents to leave work find child poverty falls substantially.{c:work-effect}

questions.q: Why do higher earners get less?
a: Because it is a benefit for working and middle-class families. The full amount goes to every family below about $150,000 for couples, and it falls gradually above that.{c:afa-phaseout}

questions.q: Is Social Security safe?
a: The act raises new money for it, and promises full benefits on time: if a trust fund would run short before that money is enough, the general fund lends it the shortfall, repaid with interest.{c:ss-act} The plan's other taxes don't touch Social Security, which keeps its own financing.{c:ss}

what_changed: Child care is free for families at or below 85% of their state's median income, and no family pays more than 7% of its income for a child too young for school, with no income limit.{c:cc-free}{c:cc-cap}
Pre-K is free for every 3- and 4-year-old, in schools, Head Start, centers and family child care alike.{c:prek}
Child care and pre-K staff earn at least $20 an hour in 2026 dollars, rising with wages, and early educators reach pay parity with elementary teachers.{c:care-wage}{c:cc-parity}
begins: Free care at or below 85% of median income, and free pre-K for 4-year-olds, from the 2030-31 school year; the 7% cap from July 2032; free pre-K for 3-year-olds by 2033-34.{c:cc-dates}
The $20 floor for child care staff from the 2030-31 school year, and pay parity by the 2036-37 school year.{c:care-wage}{c:cc-parity}
cost: Child care, pre-K, long-term care and the care workforce together cost about $750 billion in 2040 on our estimates, about 1.4% of the economy, as priced before the financing settlement moved more of long-term care onto the states. Most of it replaces what families now pay themselves or give in unpaid care.{c:care-cost}
limits: Free care reaches about half of families with young children, on our estimates; everyone else pays up to 7% of income.{c:cc-half}{c:cc-cap}
School-age care is not made free: children 5 to 12 keep today's child care block grant.{c:school-age}

questions.q: Why not free child care for everyone?
a: Free for every family would cost more and would mostly help families who can already pay. Capping everyone else at 7% of income means no family faces a cliff.{c:cc-cap}

questions.q: Why should parents who aren't working get child care?
a: Most families with young children already have every parent working. A work test mostly catches parents who are looking for work or in school, and it adds paperwork every time a job changes.

what_changed: One public health plan for everyone who lives here with legal or registered status: hospital, doctor, prescriptions, mental health and addiction treatment, maternity, reproductive care including abortion, dental, vision and hearing. No premiums, no deductibles, no networks, and enrollment happens automatically.{c:hlt-benefits}

No charge at all for primary care, prevention, maternity, mental health or chronic-condition drugs, and none for anyone under twice the poverty line. Above that, small copays for other care, capped at about $1,000 a year on our working figure.{c:copay-cap}
Hospitals are paid a fair rate, on a five-year glide to about 1.15 times Medicare's, where employer plans paid 254% of Medicare in 2022.{c:hospital-rates}
Today's Medicare moves into the plan: its separate parts, Medicare Advantage and Medigap end for covered care on January 1, 2035, and so do Medicare's premiums.{c:medicare-end}
begins: From 2029 the 2025 law's Medicaid cuts are undone. From January 1, 2031, everyone uninsured, everyone who buys their own insurance and every child is enrolled, and people in traditional Medicare get a $5,000 yearly cap on what they pay.{c:hlt-dates}
People on Medicaid and with job-based coverage move in over 2033 to 2035, and everyone is in by January 1, 2035.{c:hlt-dates}
cost: On our estimates the country spends about $491 billion a year less on health care at full scale, while households stop paying about $1.55 trillion a year in premiums and out-of-pocket costs.{c:hlt-national}

Premiums give way to a health contribution on income: 3.80% from 2035, with nothing owed at or below 138% of poverty, rising to the full rate at 250%.{c:hc-rate} In later years the rate can move a quarter point at a time under the health fund's own rule (pending). It goes into the health fund and can pay only for health care, like the Medicare payroll tax it replaces.{c:health-fund}

The federal budget's cost rises by far more than the country saves, because the government now pays what premiums used to. The health contribution pays part of that, and the general fund pays the rest, from the taxes in the money scene at the end of the day.{c:health-fund}
limits: People with no immigration status get emergency care, not the plan, so we don't say every person in the country is covered.
Taxes go up for most people, even as premiums and deductibles go away.

questions.q: Will my taxes go up?
a: Yes, for most people. Premiums, deductibles and most copays go away, and a contribution on income takes their place, with nothing owed at or below 138% of poverty.{c:hc-rate} Across the whole plan, on our estimates, every fifth of households below the top comes out ahead on average.{c:d3} The money scene at the end of the day shows how.

questions.q: Will I wait longer for care?
a: Waits may grow at first, as the Congressional Budget Office expects for any single-payer plan. The plan starts with smaller groups, keeps a small copay where care is scarcest, pays hospitals above Medicare's rates, and pays doctors at Medicare's fee schedule with extra for primary care and rural practice.

what_changed: Help at home and the care part of nursing-home stays are part of the single public health plan, for anyone of any age who needs help with three daily activities or has a serious cognitive impairment, with no asset test and no estate recovery.{c:ltc}
The top tier of help at home is funded at the level of the care part of a nursing-home stay, so a person who needs the most help can get it at home.
Home care and nursing home workers paid with public money earn at least $20 an hour in 2026 dollars, rising with wages.{c:care-wage}
begins: A five-year bridge from 2030: more money for home care, with waiting lists reported; estate recovery ends, and Medicaid's savings limit rises to $10,000 for a single person.{c:ltc-bridge}
The $20 floor for home care and nursing home workers from January 2030.{c:care-wage}
The benefit from January 2035, with new users phased in over its first two years, the heaviest needs first.{c:ltc}
cost: Part of the care package's cost of about $750 billion in 2040, on our estimates.{c:care-cost} The states keep paying what they spend on long-term care today.{c:states-ltc}
limits: Whether a family member can be paid to give care depends on the rules in their state today, until a national study reports.{c:relatives}
It is not free long-term care: there are capped copays above twice the poverty line, and nursing-home residents pay a capped share of the care and room and board from their income.

questions.q: Will my parent lose their home to pay for a nursing home?
a: No. The plan pays for most of the care, with no asset test. Residents pay a capped share, and room and board, from their income, keep a protected allowance, and a spouse at home keeps the income they need.

questions.q: Won't care workers be hard to find?
a: Yes, and it is the hardest part. Pay comes first, because it has the best evidence for keeping workers, and new users of help at home are phased in, the heaviest needs first.

what_changed: The federal minimum wage rises in yearly steps to $17.00 an hour, then rises each year with the median wage, and never falls.{c:wage-steps}

A union is certified when a majority of workers sign cards, and can still choose an election, held within 20 days. Bargaining starts within 10 days, with mediation and then binding arbitration on a timetable.{c:card-check}
Penalties of up to $50,000 per violation, sought in federal court, and workers can sue on their own if the labor board does not act.{c:penalties}

Wage insurance: a worker who loses a job held three years and takes a lower-paid one gets half the hourly drop for each hour worked, up to $10,000 a year, for two years, unless they were fired for misconduct or quit without good cause.{c:wage-ins}

One apprenticeship line built with employers in construction, energy, care and advanced manufacturing: sponsors are paid for each apprentice they start and each one who finishes, and part of each grant pays for apprentices' tools, transport, child care and mentors, toward a target of 600,000 new apprentices a year by 2034.{c:apprentice}
begins: $9.50 on January 1, 2030, then yearly steps to $17.00 on January 1, 2035, then with the median wage.{c:wage-steps}
Card check and first-contract deadlines when the labor act is signed, about mid-2029 on the plan's timeline.{c:labor-act}
Wage insurance and stronger unemployment insurance in every state from January 1, 2031.{c:ui-dates}
cost: About $0.22 trillion over 2030-39 and about $31 billion a year from 2040 on the federal budget, on our estimates, assuming no recession.{c:work-cost} Bigger unemployment benefits are paid by employers' state taxes, which roughly double.
limits: The rules ride the labor act, the hardest vote in the plan: it needs 60 Senate votes or a change to the Senate's rules, and if it is signed after June 30, 2029, every wage step moves later.{c:labor-act}

One group keeps less of a raise for a while: on our estimates a single adult buying marketplace coverage in a state that has not expanded Medicaid keeps about 39% of a raise to $12.50 in 2032, against 59% under 2029 law, and 52-59% from 2035. The fix is still open.{c:line-cook}
The apprenticeship target is a goal, not a forecast: nothing in the evidence yet shows 600,000 a year can be reached, and the count is published each year so everyone can see.{c:apprentice}

questions.q: Won't a higher minimum wage cost jobs?
a: It may cost some. The Congressional Budget Office put $15 by 2025 at 1.3 million to 1.4 million fewer jobs; other careful studies find little or no loss in the range states have tried.{c:jobs} The floor reaches $17 in 2035, when on our estimates it is about half the national median wage, in yearly steps, with a pause if unemployment is rising.{c:wage-bite}

questions.q: Doesn't card check end the secret ballot?
a: No. A union can still choose an election, held within 20 days, and mandatory anti-union meetings end.{c:card-check}

what_changed: A million new rent awards from 2030 to 2033, paid as permanent spending so they never lapse in a budget fight, first for people with no home of their own: people who are homeless, families with children doubled up with others, and anyone leaving prison, a hospital, treatment or foster care with nowhere to go.{c:awards}{c:stage1-test}
A standing emergency fund for back rent, utilities, a deposit or moving costs, up to four months of the area's rent in a year, with legal help besides.{c:emergency}
Housing First: a home without first proving sobriety or entering treatment, with services offered.
A program for the poorest families with children, enrolling up to 300,000 families a year within a capped budget, with a right for the whole group named in law as a goal for the 2040s.{c:stage2}

Later stages in order: very low-income renters with long-term disabilities, of any age, from 2038; then a stage named in law for the 2040s, opening in 2042 at up to 400,000 households a year, for renters with the lowest incomes and the worst needs who no earlier stage reaches, single adults among them. The bill states that stage and its date, but its money is enacted only with its financing.{c:later-stages}
Homes built and repaired that stay affordable for good, repairs for low-income owners, and property-tax help for older owners in states that join.
begins: Rent awards from 2030, 250,000 a year through 2033.{c:awards}
The emergency fund from 2030, with $15 billion in its first two years.{c:emergency}
The families' program from 2034, and a review in 2041 of making it a right.{c:stage2}
Renters with disabilities from 2038; the stage for the 2040s opens in 2042 if its money is enacted.{c:later-stages}
cost: About $0.81 trillion over 2030-39 and about $110 billion in 2040 as first priced, on our estimates. Capping the families' program in the financing settlement lowers the 2040 figure by about $18.6 billion.{c:home-cost}
limits: A single adult who pays most of his income in rent, but is not homeless, not disabled and not raising children, has no funded route to rent help beyond the emergency fund in a crisis.{c:not-reached}

An adult without children who lives with family is not counted as without a home, so does not qualify for the first awards. The exception is a year after leaving prison, jail or foster care for a relative's or friend's home. Someone who comes home from treatment to their parents is not covered by it.{c:stage1-test}
The stage for the 2040s reaches only people who rent, and it is not paid for: the bill names it and its date, and a later Congress has to enact the money.{c:later-stages}

Vouchers help only if families can use them. The plan assumes 90% of awards lead to a lease; the closest recent program reached 67% after about two years. That is the plan's weakest number.{c:leaseup}
The program for the poorest families is capped: families compete by need, not by right, until a later Congress votes to make it a right.{c:stage2}

questions.q: Does this end homelessness?
a: No one should promise that. For a family that gets a voucher, the effect is large and well tested. How far the national count falls is unknown, because people keep losing homes.

questions.q: Will landlords take the vouchers?
a: Housing agencies are paid their full fees for the new awards so they can recruit landlords, search help comes with every award, and a national rule would make it illegal to turn someone away just for paying with a voucher. That rule needs a regular bill to pass.

what_changed: Power plants and large factories pay for the carbon they put in the air, and most of the money comes back to every adult as a Climate Dividend, paid four times a year, tax-free, with the first payment going out before the price begins. There is no carbon charge on your gas bill or at the pump.{c:carbon-price}
Clean power and the grid built faster: a clean electricity standard of 80% by 2035 and 100% by 2040, and a public builder for needed lines no one else will build.{c:ces}
Help with energy bills that comes to you: a credit for households already getting SNAP, SSI or energy help, with no new application.
Money for every state and tribe to prepare for disasters, and a federal backstop for insurers in a catastrophic year.

A guarantee for workers when a mine, power plant or refinery closes: up to 90% of their old pay for two years, in a new job or in training, and lost local tax revenue replaced in full at first, then a little less each year for ten years.{c:guarantee}
begins: The carbon price from 2030, at $25 a ton, reaching $150 by 2037.{c:carbon-price}
The bill credit from the winter of 2030-31.{c:bill-credit}
The worker guarantee for closures from 2030.{c:guarantee}
cost: About $1.73 trillion over 2030-39 on our estimates, a little below what the plan first set aside for these purposes, and less after that, as the clean-energy credits step down under the law to nothing by 2047.{c:power-cost}{c:credits-end}
On our estimates the dividend is about $405 an adult in 2035, in that year's dollars; it moves with what polluters pay, and shrinks as pollution falls.{c:dividend}
limits: Electricity costs somewhat more while the clean grid is built: on our estimates the average price is about a tenth higher than under current law by 2040. On the carbon price and the dividend alone, on our estimates, the lowest-income two-fifths of households come out ahead on average, nationally, though some in states that burn the most coal may be behind.{c:bills}

The clean electricity standard is a target. On our estimates the grid reaches about 73% clean power in 2035 and 87% in 2040, held back by connections to the grid, and suppliers that fall short pay a capped fee.{c:ces-model}
It does not reach the 2035 climate goal, a 61-66% cut from 2005, on its own: on our estimates carbon emissions from energy fall about 41% below 2005 by 2035.{c:emissions}
The worker guarantee covers closures, not every oil and gas job.

questions.q: Isn't this a carbon tax?
a: It is a price on the biggest polluters: power plants and large industrial facilities. Households pay no charge of their own, and most of the money goes back to every adult, with the first payment made before the price begins.

questions.q: Didn't Canada try this and drop it?
a: Canada dropped its charge on consumers and kept the price on large emitters. This plan is the part Canada kept.

what_changed: Earned legal status: people who have lived here ten years or more get a green card after fingerprints and a criminal check, and so do Dreamers and people who have held temporary protection. Everyone else here on the day the law is signed can register, work legally and be protected from deportation while they reach ten years.{c:earned}
Legal lines fixed: more family and employment green cards, and spouses and children of permanent residents no longer wait in line.
Trained asylum officers decide claims within 180 days of filing, and in about 90 days in a surge, with more officers instead of a ban on asking for protection.{c:asylum}

ICE is replaced, enforcement is focused by law on threats to security, serious crime and recent unlawful entry, and no more than 30,000 people are held on average, outside a declared surge.{c:detention}
begins: Filing for legal status from late 2030.{c:imm-dates}
Workplace checks with E-Verify no earlier than October of the year after the law passes, and only once an independent inspector confirms legal status is up and running.{c:everify}
cost: About $0.16 trillion over 2030-39 and about $24.6 billion in 2040, on our estimates.{c:imm-cost}
limits: Surges will still happen. The plan meets them with more officers and a faster track, not a promise that they stop.
Not everyone who qualifies will apply; our estimates assume about 70% do.{c:takeup}

questions.q: Isn't this amnesty?
a: It is earned status, by two routes. Dreamers, people who have held temporary protection, DACA or parole, and farm, care and construction workers with a work history get a green card on approval, after fingerprints and a criminal check.{c:earned} Everyone else here earns it after ten years' residence, under the registry already in immigration law, whose date has been stuck at 1972 since 1986.{c:registry}

questions.q: Will my information be used to deport my family?
a: No. The law bars using registration or program records for immigration enforcement, with penalties, except under a criminal warrant for a named person.

what_changed: Registration done by the state from records it already holds, with a mailed notice and a way to decline; any current government, tribal, student or benefit card as identification, or a signed statement; mail voting without an excuse and at least two weeks of early voting.
Preclearance returns for places with a record of recent violations, and until the next census redistricting no state may redraw its congressional map in the middle of a decade.

Small in-state gifts up to $200 matched six to one for House and Senate candidates who opt in. The match is voluntary: to qualify, a candidate raises a set number of small in-state gifts and accepts a lower limit on the gifts they take.{c:match}
No individual stocks for members of Congress and top officials, without a forced sale; a binding code for the Justices and eighteen-year terms for future Justices, when the politics allow.
The agencies every other promise runs through are rebuilt, about 54,000 added staff across six of them, with money released as each agency hires.{c:rebuild}
begins: The voting floor from the first federal general election at least 180 days after the democracy act: November 5, 2030, if it is law by May 9, 2030.{c:dem-start}
Matched small gifts from the 2032 elections on the plan's working timeline.{c:match}
The agency rebuild in the first budget act of 2029.{c:rebuild}
cost: About $503 billion over 2030-39 and $51.6 billion in 2040, on our estimates, about three-quarters of it the agency rebuild.{c:dem-cost}
limits: Most of this needs 60 Senate votes or a change to the Senate's rules.{c:dem-votes}
Some of it may be struck down in court. Each risky part is written to fall alone, so the rest stands.
No turnout gain is promised: each rule's effect comes from separate studies, and rules interact.
The match reaches only candidates who choose it; a candidate who would rather rely on large gifts can still do so, under the usual limits.{c:match}

questions.q: Isn't the stock ban a forced sale?
a: No. A covered official complies by holding diversified funds, by a qualified blind trust, or by selling, with no immediate tax on a sale made to comply.

questions.q: Why rebuild the agencies first?
a: Because every other promise runs through them. A child benefit, a health plan or a rent award is only as good as the office that delivers it, so the money is released as each agency hires against a published path.

what_changed: Repair first, with states publishing which roads and bridges are falling behind: a program to rebuild the Interstate and its bridges, help to keep transit running in big cities, and passenger rail paid out only as projects prove they are ready.

The gas tax rises with prices, plus ten small steps, then five more over 2040-44, each pausing when gas prices spike.{c:fuel-steps} Electric cars pay by the mile, at what an efficient gas car pays, read from the odometer, with no tracking device.
The heaviest trucks pay by weight and miles, instead of a flat $550 that hasn't changed since 1984.{c:trucks}
begins: The new fuel and mileage charges start first; the 2031 transportation law takes effect on October 1, 2031, with its outright ban on collecting location data.{c:mov-dates}
cost: For a typical gas car, federal fuel tax goes from $88 a year today to $225 in 2036, on our estimates; an electric car pays $141.{c:fuel-cost}
limits: Our figures assume people don't drive less when fuel taxes rise, so the revenue is an upper bound.
The plan narrows the Interstate's repair gap; it does not close it.

questions.q: Will the government track my car?
a: No. The charge reads only the odometer, the readings are private tax information, and the law bans collecting location data outright and deletes readings after three years.{c:mov-dates}

what_changed: The top end and corporations pay first: the corporate rate rises to 28%, the top income tax rate returns to 39.6% for the highest earners, a new 45% bracket applies to incomes in the millions, and the 2025 law's tax cuts are reversed at the top.{c:top-rows}

On our estimates the top 1% and corporations bear 61% of the plan's new general revenue over 2030-39, leaving out the health contribution that replaces premiums, with the later steps below counted.{c:mix}

Premiums give way to a health contribution on income: 3.80% from 2035, with nothing owed at or below 138% of poverty, rising to the full rate at 250%.{c:hc-rate} In later years the rate can move a quarter point at a time under the health fund's own rule (pending). It replaces the Medicare payroll tax and works like it: it goes into the health fund, pays only for the health system, and is never spent on anything else in the budget. The general fund pays the rest of health's cost.{c:health-fund} A separate payroll contribution of 1.65 points funds the education fund.{c:edu}

Spending gives way too, across the whole federal budget: the plan drops its own $300 adult credit, the states keep paying their full current share of long-term care, defense is held flat after inflation after 2036 and restructured, crop insurance is reformed for the insurers and the largest farms, and a tax break for real-estate investors ends.{c:cuts}

On our estimates, with the later steps below counted, the plan's new spending is covered by its taxes, its savings elsewhere in the budget and the states' payments in 2035 and every year from 2039 to 2056; 2036-38 run short while the value-added tax phases in. That is not the same as a balanced federal budget.{c:closes}
The debt: the plan's chosen path has the national debt falling to 110% of the economy by 2056. With the later steps below counted, it is about 114.5% in 2040 and 110% in 2056.{c:debt-path}

The later steps that pay for that path: limits on itemized deductions and a surtax of 2 points on income above $100K for a single filer and $200K for a couple; and a value-added tax on what people buy of 2.88%, enacted in the 2033-34 Congress to start in 2035. Its rebate, $150 an adult for each point, goes in full to people under $60K of income ($120K for a couple) and phases out by $80K ($160K).{c:later-steps}{c:vat}
Nothing new in those steps reaches the middle class before 2035, so the plan's first years are paid for by the top end, corporations and savings.{c:populist}
The plan would repeal the debt limit in 2029, so it no longer stands in the way of paying bills Congress has already run up.{c:debt-limit}

questions.q: Is it paid for?
a: On our central estimates the plan as booked, its later steps counted, covers its new spending in 2035 and every year from 2039 on, with its own taxes, savings and state payments, and the top end and corporations paying first; 2036-38 run short.{c:closes} The same steps, a value-added tax among them, bring the debt down to 110% of the economy by 2056.{c:debt-path}

questions.q: Who pays?
a: Corporations and the highest earners first. Then a health contribution on income, which replaces premiums and deductibles, exempts people at or below 138% of poverty, and pays only for health care.{c:hc-rate}{c:health-fund} Then savings across the rest of the federal budget, defense included. From 2035, a value-added tax of 2.88% with a rebate for people below an income line.{c:vat}

questions.q: Why a value-added tax, and why wait?
a: The other choice was a higher health contribution, which on our estimates does somewhat better for low-income workers. But the plan keeps that contribution for health care's own cost, with its rate set by the health fund's own rule, so the debt path is paid for by other steps, a value-added tax among them.{c:health-fund}{c:vat-vs-r} The tax waits until 2035 so nothing new reaches the middle class in the plan's first years.{c:populist} Its rebate goes only to people below an income line, to keep the help for low and middle incomes: in full under $60K of income ($120K for a couple), phased out by $80K ($160K).{c:vat}

families.name: Jordan
families.about: A single man in his mid-twenties, learning a trade and renting a room across town.

moments.place: A job site at the edge of town
moments.title: A trade, and a contract
moments.illustration: Early light over a fenced job site where a new battery building for the grid is going up. A young man in a hard hat and tool belt pulls cable with an older electrician; a union sticker on his lunch cooler.

beats.text: Jordan is in the second year of a registered apprenticeship, wiring a new battery building for the power grid. His sponsor is paid for each apprentice it starts and each one who finishes, and part of that money bought his tools and his bus pass.
His crew voted in their union by signing cards, and their first contract came on a deadline instead of after years of delay.

moments.title: Stitches, and a small copay
moments.illustration: A bright clinic room. A young man in work clothes holds out a bandaged hand to a nurse; his hard hat sits on the chair beside him.

beats.text: Jordan slices his hand on a panel edge and gets three stitches at urgent care. He has been in the public plan since he was a kid and has never seen a premium or a deductible. Because he earns more than twice the poverty line, he pays a small copay, capped for the year.

moments.place: The job site, as a storm comes in
moments.title: Storm call
moments.illustration: Dark clouds roll over the job site. Workers lash down cable reels; a young man checks his phone, where a payment notice glows.

beats.text: The crew ties down before the storm. Jordan's Climate Dividend landed last week, as it does four times a year: power plants and big factories pay for the carbon they put in the air, and most of that money comes back to every adult.

moments.title: Dani's oath
moments.illustration: A plain hearing room with flags. A young woman raises her right hand among a row of new citizens; a friend in work clothes holds up a phone to take her picture.

beats.text: Jordan's roommate Dani was brought here as a child. When the law passed she got her green card on approval, after fingerprints and a criminal check. Today she takes the oath as a citizen, and Jordan came straight from work to take the picture.
Down the hall, a family that crossed the border in last spring's surge hears the decision on their asylum claim, a few months after they filed, not years.

moments.place: A rented room in a shared apartment
moments.title: The rent is still the hard part
moments.illustration: A small bedroom in a shared apartment: a mattress, a desk with a laptop open to a budget, work boots by the door.

beats.text: Rent takes the biggest bite of Jordan's pay. The plan's rent help goes first to people with no home of their own, then to the poorest families with children and renters with disabilities. A single worker like him, who isn't homeless, isn't disabled and isn't raising children, has no funded route to rent help.
What reaches him is slower: more homes built that stay affordable for good, and the emergency fund if a crisis hits.

moments.title: Twenty-five dollars, matched
moments.illustration: A library meeting room with folding chairs. A candidate speaks at the front; a young man near the back holds a printed flyer.

beats.text: Jordan stops by a candidate forum at the library. He was registered to vote automatically from his driver's license record, and he gave $25 to the House candidate speaking tonight. She opted in to the small-gift match, so his gift brought her campaign $175.{c:match}

moments.title: The route that survived
moments.illustration: The inside of a city bus at night, half full. A young man leans his head on the window; a repaired bridge passes outside, lit by new lamps.

beats.text: Jordan rides the bus home. The route survived because the city kept its own funding to qualify for help with running costs, and the bridge on the way was repaired, on a list of bridges the state publishes.

moments.title: What it costs, and who pays
moments.illustration: A phone screen in a dark room, showing a pay stub. The city lights beyond the window.

beats.text: Before bed Jordan checks his pay stub. There is no premium on it. There is the health contribution on his income, which goes into the health fund and can pay only for health care.

families.name: Maya and Sam
families.about: A couple in their thirties with two young children, Theo and Nora. Sam's aging parents, Hector and Lupe, live a few blocks away.

moments.title: The money comes on the first
moments.illustration: Early light in a small kitchen. A mother in a robe holds a newborn on her shoulder while checking a phone; a father pours cereal for a four-year-old still in pajamas.

beats.text: The phone buzzes before the coffee is ready: the child benefit for Theo and Nora is in, as it is on the first of every month. Maya and Sam never applied for it. It started from the children's birth records.
Maya is home with Nora on paid leave, at most of her pay, and her job is waiting for her when she goes back.

moments.place: The pre-K classroom at the neighborhood school
moments.title: Pre-K, and a cap on what care costs
moments.illustration: A bright classroom of small tables. A father kneels to zip a little boy's jacket off; a teacher waves from a reading rug.

beats.text: Sam walks Theo to pre-K at the school down the street. It is free for every three- and four-year-old.

When Nora starts child care next fall, Maya and Sam earn too much for it to be free. But no family pays more than 7% of its income for a child too young for school, so they know the most it will cost.{c:cc-cap}

moments.title: A checkup with nothing to pay
moments.illustration: A pediatric exam room with a baby scale. A mother holds her newborn while a doctor listens with a stethoscope.

beats.text: Nora's newborn checkup costs nothing, and neither did her birth: maternity care, newborn care and primary care are free for everyone in the plan.

moments.title: Help at home, savings intact
moments.illustration: A tidy living room with family photos. A home care aide helps an older woman with a cardigan; an older man sets out two cups of tea.

beats.text: An aide arrives to help Lupe through her morning. Nobody asked Hector and Lupe to spend down their savings first: long-term care is part of the public health plan, with no asset test.
Sam calls between shifts. He no longer worries that caring for his mother will cost his parents their house.

moments.title: A photo on the fridge
moments.illustration: A refrigerator door covered in grandchildren's drawings and, in the middle, a framed photo of a man holding up a green card.

beats.text: On the fridge is a photo of Hector the day he got his green card. He had lived and worked here for decades. He proved his years from tax records the government already held, passed a fingerprint and criminal check, and a few years later he became a citizen.

moments.title: A raise that keeps up
moments.illustration: A break room with lockers and a vending machine. A man in a safety vest reads a pay stub; a union notice is pinned to the board behind him.

beats.text: On his break Sam looks over the new hires' pay. The wage floor went up again this January, as it does every year with the median wage, so a raise never waits for Congress.
His coworkers voted in their union by signing cards, and their first contract came on a deadline.

moments.place: The front porch, as a storm comes in
moments.title: Storm season, dividend day
moments.illustration: A front porch with a stroller and a tricycle. A woman holding a baby watches dark clouds; a utility truck passes on the street.

beats.text: Maya watches the storm roll in. Two Climate Dividends, hers and Sam's, came this quarter, and there has never been a carbon charge on their gas bill.

moments.title: Paying by the mile, without being tracked
moments.illustration: A small electric car at a stoplight in evening traffic, a car seat visible in the back; a dashboard odometer in close-up.

beats.text: Sam drives home in the family's electric car. It pays its share of the roads by the mile, at what an efficient gas car pays, read from the odometer, with no tracking device.

moments.title: What it costs, and who pays
moments.illustration: A kitchen table after the children are asleep: a laptop, a stack of bills, two mugs, a baby monitor.

beats.text: After the children are asleep, Maya and Sam go over the month: no premiums, no deductibles, child care capped, the child benefit in. Their taxes are higher than their parents' were. On our estimates every fifth of households below the top comes out ahead on average, but an average isn't a promise for any one family.{c:d3}

families.name: Carol and Dev
families.about: A couple getting ready to retire. Their adult son, Eli, struggled with substance use and lives with them because he can't afford a place of his own. They want to help their family, and they also plan to enjoy their retirement.

moments.title: Full benefits, on time
moments.illustration: A morning kitchen. A woman in reading glasses holds a printed statement; her husband reads over her shoulder; their grown son, in a work jacket, grabs a travel mug on his way out.

beats.text: Carol opens her Social Security statement: the full benefit she earned, on time. A 2030 act raised the money to keep it that way, and if a trust fund had ever run short first, the law has the general fund lend it the difference.{c:ss-act}
Eli heads out to a paid training program in home repair. He gets a stipend for the weeks he trains, and nothing else he gets depends on taking part.

moments.title: Treatment, covered like any other care
moments.illustration: A calm clinic waiting room with plants and a counselor's door ajar. A man in his thirties signs in at the desk; nobody asks for a card.

beats.text: Eli checks in for counseling and the medication that keeps him in recovery. The plan covers addiction treatment as it covers any other care, and he has no premium or deductible to pay.
Turning sixty-five next year changes nothing about Dev's coverage: no Medicare sign-up, no premium to pay, no extra policy to shop for. The plan he has had for years just continues.

moments.title: Planning the trip
moments.illustration: A kitchen table covered in a map and travel brochures. An older couple point at a coastline, laughing.

beats.text: Carol and Dev are planning their first long trip in years. They don't have to keep their savings untouched against a nursing home: if one of them someday needs help with daily life, long-term care is part of the public plan, with no asset test.

moments.title: A room at his parents', for now
moments.illustration: A spare bedroom in a family house, a little crowded: a single bed, a toolbox, a calendar with recovery meetings circled, an apartment listing printed on the desk.

beats.text: Eli would like a place of his own, and he can't afford one yet. He doesn't qualify for the plan's first rent awards. They go to people with no home of their own, and adults staying with family count only if they have children, or for a year after leaving prison, jail or foster care. Coming home from treatment to his parents' house doesn't count.

The later stages reach the poorest families with children, then very low-income renters with disabilities. The plan names one more stage in law, for single renters with the lowest incomes and the worst rent burdens, but it isn't paid for yet, and it helps people who already rent. For now his parents' spare room is home, and Carol and Dev are glad to have him.

moments.place: The front porch, as a storm comes in
moments.title: Dividends with the check
moments.illustration: An older couple on a porch swing under a darkening sky, a dog at their feet, a tablet showing a deposit notice.

beats.text: Carol and Dev watch the storm roll in. Their Climate Dividends come four times a year, and when they claim Social Security, the dividends will come with their checks.

moments.title: Someone picks up
moments.illustration: A man on a landline in a hallway, a notepad in his hand, a Social Security envelope open on the side table.

beats.text: Dev calls Social Security to ask when he should start his benefit, and someone picks up. The office is staffed again.

moments.title: What it costs, and who pays
moments.illustration: A living room lit by one lamp. An older couple on a couch with a notebook of figures; a third mug on the table for their son.

beats.text: Carol and Dev go over their retirement plan: Social Security in full, no Medicare premiums, and the health contribution on their income in place of them. They want to enjoy the years ahead, and they set a little aside to help Eli with a deposit when the time comes.
